paragraphs: Large data pipelines often replace raw data with compact summaries called sketches. This paper studies sketches that support sampling and statistical estimation based on how frequently items occur. The summaries must also be composable, so information summarized separately can be combined. Some useful frequency functions, including thresholds and frequency moments above order two, require polynomial storage in the worst case.

The authors investigate whether smaller summaries become possible under two different kinds of additional information. One setting provides noisy advice about item frequencies, potentially supplied by a learned predictor. The other restricts the input frequency distributions to classes that better reflect patterns observed in practice. These are distinct ways of moving beyond guarantees that must accommodate every possible input.

Their analytical and empirical results show that small, polylogarithmic sketches can accurately handle functions considered difficult under worst-case analysis. The significance is conditional: predictions or distributional structure can make compact summaries effective without overturning the general worst-case storage requirements.
icml-2020-composable-sketches-for-functi.tldr: Noisy frequency predictions or restrictions on input distributions can enable compact sketches for functions that require much larger summaries in the worst case.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning represents uncertainty through a posterior distribution, but computing that distribution exactly can be impractical. Variational inference replaces it with an approximation that is easier to work with. This paper asks whether that computational substitution sacrifices statistical performance when learning smooth functions with sparse deep neural networks.

The authors establish that, in the setting they analyze, variational inference preserves the generalization properties of exact Bayesian inference. With a suitable network architecture, the resulting estimates converge at nearly the best possible statistical rate for Hölder smooth functions, a class characterized by controlled variation. Here, convergence describes how estimation improves as more data become available, rather than how quickly an optimization routine finishes.

The paper also studies choosing the network architecture by maximizing the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. Its model selection framework avoids overfitting and adaptively attains the optimal convergence rate. Together, the results justify both posterior approximation and architecture selection within the sparse deep learning framework studied.
icml-2020-convergence-rates-of-variation.tldr: For the sparse neural networks studied, variational inference matches exact Bayesian generalization, while ELBO-based architecture selection adaptively achieves optimal convergence rates.

paragraphs: Directed graphical models describe probabilistic relationships among variables and support predictions in sensitive settings such as medical diagnosis. Learning their parameters privately requires protecting information about the training data while preserving useful inference. This paper develops a differentially private parameter learning algorithm with the usefulness of subsequent inference queries as its central objective.

The method customizes added noise to both the private dataset and the model's graph structure. Its privacy budget allocation therefore responds to characteristics of the particular learning problem. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first explicit data-dependent allocation algorithm for directed graphical models. The contribution concerns how to distribute the privacy budget while maintaining the stated privacy protection.

Across the reported benchmark suite, the algorithm achieves equal or better utility with a privacy budget roughly three times smaller than a standard data-independent approach requires. This empirical finding suggests that accounting for data and graph structure can improve the privacy–utility tradeoff for the evaluated inference tasks.
icml-2020-data-dependent-differentially-.tldr: Customizing privacy noise to the dataset and graph structure delivers equal or better inference utility with roughly three times less privacy budget in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning how to compare examples can mean learning a neural representation or learning a more general measure of difference. Deep metric learning develops the representation, while Bregman divergence learning broadens the comparison beyond ordinary Euclidean distance. This paper brings these directions together by using neural networks to parameterize and learn functional Bregman divergences.

The resulting framework covers several established approaches within one mathematical construction. In the symmetric setting, the authors show that deep metric learning formulations, kernel metric learning, Mahalanobis metric learning, and moment-based comparisons between distributions arise as special cases. This connection matters because it relates methods for comparing individual representations to methods for comparing distributions.

The authors also provide a deep learning framework for learning general functional divergences. On the benchmark datasets they evaluate, it outperforms existing deep metric learning approaches. They discuss additional uses in semi-supervised clustering of distributions and an unsupervised generation loss. These applications illustrate the broader scope of learning the comparison function itself.
icml-2020-deep-divergence-learning-f08ea.tldr: Deep Bregman divergences unify several representation and distribution comparison methods and outperform existing deep metric learning approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning builds a representation in which similar examples lie closer together than dissimilar ones. Neural approaches often encourage examples from the same class to cluster tightly while separating different classes. These objectives shape how much information from the original inputs survives in the learned space, making their balance a central design issue.

The paper proposes Joint Representation Diversification to obtain a better balance between within-class compactness and between-class separation. Its main mechanism is a Joint Representation Similarity regularizer. This regularizer works across multiple network layers, capturing invariant features at different levels of abstraction and diversifying the joint distributions of those representations.

Considering multiple layers gives the method access to different levels of learned information when shaping the final distance space. Experiments on three deep metric learning benchmarks support the effectiveness of the approach. The stated finding is that this form of representation diversification improves the balance pursued by metric learning in the tested settings.
icml-2020-distance-metric-learning-with-.tldr: A regularizer spanning multiple network layers improves the balance between keeping similar examples close and separating different classes in the evaluated metric learning tasks.

paragraphs: Generating a musical sequence involves more than choosing each next event: a performance also has style and structure that extend across time. This paper addresses how to provide high-level control over those longer-range properties in symbolic music generation. Its goal is to make aspects of a generated performance more separately controllable.

The proposed Transformer autoencoder combines input encodings across time into a global representation of a performance's style. The authors show that this summary can be used alongside embeddings distributed throughout the sequence. Combining these forms of representation enables improved control over performance style and melody, which operate at different levels of the musical sequence.

The method is evaluated on multiple music generation tasks using MAESTRO and a YouTube collection containing more than 10,000 hours of piano performances. It improves both log-likelihood and average listening scores over the compared baselines. Those results support the usefulness of the representation through both a model-based measure and listeners' assessments.
icml-2020-encoding-musical-style-with-tr.tldr: A Transformer autoencoder combines global style summaries with sequence-level embeddings to improve musical control and generation quality in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A model can lose accuracy when deployed on data that differ from its training distribution, while still appearing overly confident about its performance. This paper studies how to estimate that performance without labeled target data. The practical objective is to assess a deployed model when its actual test errors cannot be measured directly.

The method uses a collection of domain-invariant predictors as substitutes for the unavailable target labels. These proxy predictions provide a way to estimate risk, but the estimate's error depends on how well the proxy model itself performs on the target distribution. The authors therefore analyze domain-invariant representations and show that the complexity of the latent representation substantially influences target risk.

Empirically, the approach accurately estimates target error in the evaluated distribution shifts and enables domain adaptation models to tune themselves. The authors also identify model selection, early stopping, and error detection as applications. The proxy dependence explains why representation quality matters both for prediction and for evaluating other models.
icml-2020-estimating-generalization-unde.tldr: Domain-invariant proxy predictors estimate performance without target labels, with estimation quality depending on the proxies' own target performance.

paragraphs: A generative model trained on a demographically biased dataset may reproduce its imbalance. Addressing this is difficult in unsupervised learning because the factors associated with bias may not be explicitly labeled. This paper introduces a weakly supervised method that uses a small additional reference dataset as guidance without requiring labels for those underlying factors.

The method compares the biased and reference datasets through a density ratio technique to detect distributional bias. It then learns from examples in both datasets, combining the larger training collection with the reference signal. The intended output distribution is close to the reference dataset's distribution, so that reference supplies the direction of the correction.

In image generation experiments with generative adversarial networks, the authors report average bias reductions of up to 34.6% relative to baselines for comparable generation. The result supports using a small unlabeled reference collection to improve the evaluated bias measures while retaining data from the original collection for training.
icml-2020-fair-generative-modeling-via-w.tldr: A small unlabeled reference dataset guides generative training toward its distribution, reducing measured latent-factor bias in the reported image experiments.

paragraphs: Online knowledge distillation lets networks learn from one another while they are trained together. Earlier methods described in this paper transfer class probabilities, leaving information in internal feature maps unused. Those maps also contain image intensity and spatial relationships, motivating a method that shares both output predictions and internal representations.

The authors use adversarial training to transfer feature map distributions. Each network has a discriminator trained to treat its own network's maps as fake and another network's maps as real. The network learns to fool that discriminator, encouraging its feature distribution to resemble its peer's. A cyclic learning arrangement extends the approach to groups larger than two networks.

The reported comparisons favor this distribution-based transfer over direct feature alignment such as an L1 penalty for online distillation. Classification experiments across several network architectures show performance improvements, especially when a small network trains alongside a large one. The findings support sharing richer internal information during simultaneous training.
icml-2020-feature-map-level-online-adver.tldr: Adversarially matching feature map distributions improves online knowledge distillation, particularly for a small network trained alongside a larger one.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer Bayesian predictions, but their cubic training cost motivates splitting data among smaller local experts. Product-of-experts methods combine the resulting predictive distributions using a tractable multiplication operation. This supports highly distributed computation, yet the combined predictions can have unstable means or uncertainty estimates that are poorly calibrated.

The paper addresses these problems by calibrating expert predictions with tempered softmax weighting. This changes how the individual experts contribute to the aggregate prediction. The authors provide the approach for multiple product-of-experts models, including the generalized product of experts and the robust Bayesian committee machine, making it relevant to several existing aggregation choices.

They also introduce an expert combination model based on optimal transport. It forms the combined prediction through a Wasserstein barycenter, a way of averaging distributions using Wasserstein geometry. The proposed model applies to regression and classification. Together, the contributions focus on improving how local predictions are combined so distributed Gaussian process modeling can provide more dependable outputs.
icml-2020-healing-products-of-gaussian-p.tldr: Tempered expert weighting addresses unstable Gaussian process predictions, and a Wasserstein barycenter provides an additional way to combine local experts.

paragraphs: Fair data summarization must account for fairness while producing a compact representation of a large collection. This paper studies that objective through the fair k-center problem. Its algorithms target streaming and distributed computation, where datasets can be processed without requiring the full collection to fit into a single machine's main memory.

The authors give the first distributed algorithm for the problem with a provable constant approximation ratio and substantial parallelism. They also develop a streaming algorithm that makes two passes over the data. Its approximation guarantee matches the best previously known algorithm, even though that comparison algorithm does not operate in the streaming setting.

The proposed methods have linear running times and small working memory and communication requirements. Evaluations on real and synthetic datasets show improvements over existing algorithms. A complementary hardness result identifies limits for natural distributed algorithms, even for ordinary k-center. The contributions therefore pair scalable approximation methods with evidence about constraints on distributed approaches.
icml-2020-how-to-solve-fair-k-center-in-.tldr: New distributed and two-pass streaming algorithms provide provable fair k-center approximations with small resource requirements and strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: The k-means++ algorithm has a known approximation guarantee whose factor grows logarithmically with the number of clusters, k. A constant approximation gives a bound that does not grow with k. This paper investigates how much additional local search is needed to strengthen the k-means++ guarantee in that way.

Previous analysis obtained a constant approximation in expectation after adding O(k log log k) local search steps. The authors improve the analysis to show that only epsilon times k additional steps suffice, for any chosen positive constant epsilon, however small. Their guarantee holds with high probability as a function of k, strengthening the type of assurance as well as reducing the required step count.

The result resolves an open problem about the augmented algorithm. Its significance is a sharper theoretical account of what a short local search phase can achieve after k-means++: even a small constant proportion of k additional steps can yield a constant-factor bound.
icml-2020-k-means-few-more-steps-yield-c.tldr: For any fixed positive epsilon, adding only epsilon times k local search steps to k-means++ yields a constant approximation with high probability in k.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning benchmarks need to measure both how efficiently agents learn and how well their learning transfers across environments. This paper introduces Procgen Benchmark, a collection of 16 game-like environments created through procedural generation. Generating environments supplies varied experiences for studying sample efficiency and generalization within the same benchmark suite.

The authors provide detailed experimental protocols to support training and evaluation with the benchmark. Their experiments demonstrate the importance of diverse environment distributions for adequately training and assessing agents. This evidence motivates procedural content generation as a way to supply the variation needed to investigate these capabilities, with environment diversity playing a central role in the evaluation design.

The paper also uses Procgen to examine the effect of increasing model size. In the reported experiments, larger models significantly improve both sample efficiency and generalization. The contribution thus includes a benchmark and an empirical finding about capacity: under the studied conditions, larger models learn more efficiently and generalize better.
icml-2020-leveraging-procedural-generati.tldr: Procgen provides 16 procedurally generated environments and shows that environment diversity and larger models improve reinforcement learning evaluation and performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Models trained on heterogeneous datasets can produce separate posterior distributions that need to be combined. This paper proposes a method for fusing those distributions into a global model. It assumes a mean field form for both the individual posteriors and the fused posterior, so the method operates on their factorized components.

The algorithm alternates between assigning and averaging. First, it matches components from the dataset-specific posteriors to components of the proposed global model by solving a regularized assignment problem. It then updates the global components using a mean defined through Kullback–Leibler divergence. The matching step establishes which local components should contribute to each global component before aggregation.

For exponential family variational distributions, this formulation yields an efficient non-parametric fusion algorithm. The authors describe it as straightforward to implement and report competitive performance in motion capture analysis, topic modeling, and federated learning of Bayesian neural networks. These applications demonstrate the method's usefulness across different posterior fusion tasks under its factorization assumption.
icml-2020-model-fusion-with-kullback-lei.tldr: Under mean field assumptions, an assign-and-average algorithm fuses dataset-specific posterior components using KL divergence and performs competitively across several applications.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small data summary used to approximate a larger regression problem. This paper asks when adding norm-based regularization permits a smaller coreset. It studies objectives combining a powered norm of the prediction residuals with a powered norm of the model parameters, in settings with many more observations than features.

The central lower bound shows that when the two powers differ, regularized regression cannot have a smaller coreset than the optimal one for its unregularized counterpart. Standard lasso falls into this category, so its regularization does not permit a smaller coreset than least squares. This identifies a precise obstruction to obtaining the storage benefit already known for ridge regression.

The authors propose a modified lasso that admits smaller coresets and empirically retains sparsity in its solutions. They also obtain smaller coresets for matched lp regression and lp regularization, and extend their methods to multiple response variables. Experiments evaluate the modified lasso and l1-regularized l1 regression constructions.
icml-2020-on-coresets-for-regularized-re.tldr: Regularization cannot shrink optimal regression coresets when the residual and penalty powers differ, but modified lasso and matched lp formulations allow smaller summaries.

paragraphs: Hierarchical representations can simplify a dataset while preserving relationships among its points. This paper studies embeddings into ultrametrics, which encode hierarchical distance structure. Computing such representations can require quadratic time, motivating an algorithm that trades some approximation quality for a more favorable dependence on dataset size.

For n points in Euclidean space, the proposed algorithm uses a parameter c of at least one and runs in time n raised to 1 plus rho divided by c squared, where rho is a universal constant greater than one. Its pairwise ultrametric distances are within a multiplicative factor of 5c of those in the best ultrametric representation. Increasing c improves the runtime exponent while loosening that guarantee.

A separate conditional hardness result concerns the l-infinity metric: under the stated complexity assumptions, truly subquadratic algorithms cannot distinguish isometric instances from ones requiring distortion of 3/2. Empirical evaluations show outputs comparable to linkage algorithms with much faster runtimes. The theoretical upper and lower results address different underlying metrics.
icml-2020-on-efficient-low-distortion-ul.tldr: A tunable algorithm trades ultrametric approximation quality for speed, with empirical results comparable to linkage methods and a separate conditional hardness result for l-infinity inputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when both rewards and state transition distributions change over time. The setting is undiscounted, and the total amount of change is bounded by variation budgets. The challenge is to keep learning effectively as the environment drifts, with performance measured through dynamic regret.

The first algorithm, SWUCRL2-CW, combines a sliding window with upper-confidence exploration and a technique called confidence widening. The authors establish a dynamic regret bound when the variation budgets are known. Confidence widening introduces additional optimism to address a difficulty specific to learning drifting Markov decision processes, where conventional optimistic exploration encounters challenges absent from the corresponding bandit setting.

The second algorithm, BORL, adaptively tunes the sliding window without knowing the variation budgets. It achieves the same stated dynamic regret bound in this parameter-free sense. Together, the methods show how additional optimism and adaptive window selection can support learning under bounded environmental drift, including when the amount of drift is not supplied beforehand.
icml-2020-reinforcement-learning-for-non.tldr: Confidence widening enables regret guarantees for drifting Markov decision processes, while adaptive window tuning achieves the same bound without knowing the variation budgets.

paragraphs: Comparison-based search locates a target by repeatedly asking which of two objects is more similar to it. This paper considers noisy answers generated from latent object features. It separates the problem into a setting where the search algorithm can access those features and a harder setting where the features are hidden.

With accessible features, the authors propose a Bayesian search algorithm designed to use few queries while keeping computation low. They derive the form of the optimal query and prove almost sure convergence to the target. For hidden features, they combine the search procedure with a new distributional triplet embedding algorithm in a framework called Learn2Search.

On two real-world datasets, Learn2Search achieves query complexity comparable to the setting with accessible features, a result the evaluated existing embedding methods do not achieve. An experiment involving real users searching for movie actors further demonstrates the framework. The findings connect learning a representation from comparisons with using that representation for efficient search.
icml-2020-scalable-and-efficient-compari.tldr: Learn2Search combines Bayesian comparison search with learned embeddings to achieve query efficiency comparable to feature-aware search on two real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Some learning problems need to select or remove whole groups of variables together. The l1,infinity norm supports this kind of structured sparsity, but optimization with its constraint is harder than with a conventional l1 constraint. This paper focuses on the Euclidean projection operation: finding the closest point that lies inside the permitted norm ball.

The authors formulate the projection through a system of semismooth equations and solve it using a semismooth Newton method. They then exploit the structure of the Jacobian matrix through LU decomposition to obtain an equivalent algorithm. For this equivalent procedure, they prove termination after a finite number of iterations, providing a theoretical property of the solver.

Empirical studies show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing state-of-the-art solver in the reported comparisons. Because projection is the specific operation being improved, the result is relevant to learning problems constrained by an l1,infinity norm ball. The authors identify such optimization problems as a promising application of the method.
icml-2020-semismooth-newton-algorithm-fo.tldr: A semismooth Newton approach efficiently projects onto the l1,infinity norm ball, with a finite-termination equivalent algorithm and favorable reported solver comparisons.

paragraphs: Some machine learning optimization problems involve orthogonal matrices or related geometric spaces. This paper develops a class of stochastic optimization algorithms guided by that geometry. The methods operate on the orthogonal group and on naturally reductive homogeneous manifolds arising from the action of the rotation group.

The authors use Lie group theory to establish theoretical results for the algorithm class. They also reveal connections between efficient stochastic optimization on the orthogonal group and graph problems, including matching, graph coloring, and partition functions. These links connect the structure of the optimization domain with tools from discrete mathematics.

The paper presents theoretical and experimental support for applications across neural networks, reinforcement learning, normalizing flows, and metric learning. Its highlighted demonstrations include learning world models to obtain stable policies for the difficult Humanoid agent in OpenAI Gym and improving convolutional networks. The reported performance supports the approach across distinct tasks, showing that geometry-driven optimization can serve several kinds of learning system.
icml-2020-stochastic-flows-and-geometric.tldr: Geometry-driven stochastic optimizers connect orthogonal-group learning with graph theory and show strong reported performance in reinforcement learning and convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization is an important component of learning pipelines, particularly those involving latent variable models. This paper asks how to support it when vectors arrive as a stream. The proposed algorithms retain a coreset containing a sublinear number of the input vectors, reducing the amount of data needed for the factorization task.

The guarantee connects the summary directly to the intended computation: the CP decomposition of its p-th moment tensor approximates the corresponding decomposition constructed from all the data. The authors introduce online filtering and kernelization to build four algorithms. These provide different balances among coreset size, update time, and working memory, matching or improving various existing methods.

For matrices, which are second-order tensors, an online row sampling algorithm gives a relative-error spectral approximation within a factor of one plus or minus epsilon. The paper also demonstrates applications to single-topic modeling. The contribution therefore combines streaming data reduction with guarantees tied to the matrix or tensor structure used downstream.
icml-2020-streaming-coresets-for-symmetr.tldr: Streaming algorithms retain sublinear subsets of vectors while preserving approximations to moment-tensor decompositions, with several memory and update-time tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search usually needs a representation of the dataset that can answer later queries. This paper presents an online sketch that compresses the data into short integer arrays while retaining the ability to report nearest neighbors. The authors identify it as the first such sketch with sublinear memory.

For N data elements, its storage is O(N^b log^3 N), with b less than one, and its construction time is O(N^(b+1) log^3 N). Correct retrieval is guaranteed for queries satisfying a stability condition parameterized by b. The method combines locality-sensitive-hashing estimators, online kernel density estimation, and compressed sensing to obtain this conditional memory guarantee.

The stability requirement is central to the result: the theorem applies to a specified class of queries. On a friend recommendation task using the Google Plus network, the authors evaluate memory against recall. They report orders-of-magnitude better compression than a random-projection alternative while preserving nearest-neighbor retrieval for practical queries in that evaluation.
icml-2020-sub-linear-memory-sketches-for.tldr: An online sketch uses sublinear memory to recover nearest neighbors for queries satisfying a stability condition and achieves strong compression in a friend recommendation evaluation.

paragraphs: Machine teaching studies how a teacher can efficiently guide a learner toward a desired hypothesis. This paper examines interactive teaching when the learner is a black box: the teacher does not know its algorithm or hypothesis class. In the starting model, the only relevant knowledge is that the target hypothesis belongs to that class.

The authors refine existing results and then relax parts of this setup. One variant allows the target to be unavailable to the learner, so the teaching objective becomes convergence to the best available approximation. Other variants consider learners whose choice among hypotheses consistent with the examples is not adversarial.

Better provable bounds are obtained for learners that favor hypotheses close to their current one and for learners that return a random consistent hypothesis. The paper also evaluates its basic interactive teacher on real datasets. Its central contribution is to show how teaching guarantees change with target availability and specific forms of learner behavior, even when the learner's internal algorithm remains unknown.
icml-2020-teaching-with-limited-informat.tldr: The paper extends black-box machine teaching to approximate targets and proves better bounds for learners that change hypotheses smoothly or select them randomly.

paragraphs: An unbiased estimate of training risk can seem like a strong foundation for learning from weak supervision. Yet such estimators can lead complex models to overfit. This paper investigates that problem through complementary-label learning, where supervision indicates a class an example does not belong to, and focuses on the gradients used during optimization.

The authors show theoretically that an unbiased risk estimator also provides an unbiased gradient estimator. However, an unbiased gradient can still have very large variance. In practice, the resulting empirical gradients may be far from the true gradients, so correctness on average does not ensure useful update directions during a particular training process.

Their surrogate complementary loss framework accepts some bias in exchange for lower variance. This makes empirical gradient directions more closely aligned with the true ones. The reported results show reduced overfitting and improvements over methods based on unbiased risk estimation. The lesson concerns optimization quality: gradient variability can matter more than maintaining zero bias in the risk estimate.
icml-2020-unbiased-risk-estimators-can-m.tldr: For complementary-label learning, accepting biased losses can reduce gradient variance, improve update directions, and mitigate overfitting.

paragraphs: Speech recognition can predict complete words or construct them from smaller units. This paper proposes a direct-to-word sequence model whose word representations are learned from letters. A dedicated word network creates these embeddings, connecting word-level prediction with the internal spelling structure of the words being represented.

The word network can be integrated with different sequence modeling approaches, including Connectionist Temporal Classification and attention-based encoder-decoder models. The authors show that the resulting model can improve word error rate over subword models. They also demonstrate that it retains the ability to predict words absent from training without requiring retraining, an important capability for a recognizer operating at word level.

A further finding concerns computational efficiency. The word-level model can use a larger stride than a subword model while maintaining accuracy, making both training and inference more efficient. Together, the results show that letter-derived word embeddings can support direct word prediction while retaining flexibility for previously unseen words and enabling coarser processing steps.
icml-2020-word-level-speech-recognition-.tldr: Letter-derived word embeddings enable direct word recognition with reported accuracy gains, prediction of unseen words without retraining, and more efficient training and inference.
